ResearchDossier.topic: the candy cane origin story is probably made up
ResearchDossier.summary: A common story says a Cologne Cathedral choirmaster bent sugar sticks into canes in 1670, shaped like shepherd's crooks; references to it don't exist before the mid-20th century and it is likely apocryphal. The earliest documented 'candy cane' is in an 1866 story in Ballou's Monthly Magazine. A recipe for striped peppermint candy sticks appeared in 1844. Robert McCormack began making candy canes in Albany, Georgia in 1919; before machines, canes had to be bent by hand.
ResearchDossier.angle: A Christmas legend nobody wrote down until the 1900s.

Script.headline: The Candy Cane Story Is Made Up
Script.cta: Follow for more things hiding in plain sight.

lines.text: That story about where candy canes come from? It's probably made up.
It goes like this. In 1670, a choirmaster in Cologne bent sugar sticks into shepherd's crooks.
To remind children of the shepherds who visited baby Jesus.
Except nobody wrote that story down until the mid-1900s.
The first written candy cane shows up in 1866, in an American magazine story.
Striped peppermint sticks are older. A recipe from 1844 already had them.
And in 1919, a candy maker in Georgia started making canes for local kids, bending every hook by hand.

That story about where candy canes come from? It's probably made up.
The tale of a Cologne choirmaster bending sugar sticks into shepherd's crooks in 1670 doesn't appear in writing until the mid-1900s. The first written candy cane shows up in 1866; striped peppermint sticks were in an 1844 recipe.
